prompt: Find the largest positive integer $n$ with the property that $n+6(p^3+1)$ is prime whenever $p$ is a prime number such that $2\le p<n$. Justify your answer.

solutions.title: Residues mod 5 (official)
solutions.body:
**$n=5$ works:** the primes $p$ with $2\le p<5$ are $2$ and $3$, and $5+6\cdot9=59$, $5+6\cdot28=173$ are both prime.

**No $n>5$ works.** Compute $6(p^3+1)\bmod5$ for small primes:
$$p=2:\ 54\equiv4,\quad p=3:\ 168\equiv3,\quad p=5:\ 756\equiv1,\quad p=11:\ 7992\equiv2,\quad p=19:\ 41160\equiv0 .$$
Whenever one of these $p$ satisfies $p<n$ and $6(p^3+1)\equiv-n\pmod5$, the number $n+6(p^3+1)$ is a multiple of $5$ larger than $5$, hence not prime.

* $n\ge20$: all five primes are available and the residues $4,3,1,2,0$ cover every class, so some $n+6(p^3+1)$ is divisible by $5$. Fails.
* $n\le19$ with $n\ge4$: $p=2,3$ are available. $n+54$ is even if $n$ is even, and $n+168$ is divisible by $3$ if $3\mid n$; so $n$ must be coprime to $6$: $n\in\{5,7,11,13,17,19\}$.
* $n\in\{13,17,19\}$: $p=2,3,5,11$ are available, killing $n\equiv1,2,4,3\pmod 5$; but $13\equiv3$, $17\equiv2$, $19\equiv4$. Fail.
* $n=7$: $p=3$ gives $175=5\cdot35$. $n=11$: $p=2$ gives $65=5\cdot13$. Fail.

Hence the largest such $n$ is $5$. (Also $n=1,2$ satisfy the condition vacuously, and $n=3,4$ fail since $3+54=57=3\cdot19$, $4+54=58$.)

**Answer: $5$.**

prompt:
Find, and write out explicitly, a permutation $(p(1),p(2),\dots,p(20))$ of $(1,2,\dots,20)$ such that $k+p(k)$ is a power of $2$ for $k=1,2,\dots,20$, and prove that only one such permutation exists. (To illustrate, a permutation of $(1,2,3,4,5)$ such that $k+p(k)$ is a power of $2$ for $k=1,2,\dots,5$ is clearly $(1,2,5,4,3)$, because $1+1=2$, $2+2=4$, $3+5=8$, $4+4=8$, and $5+3=8$.)

Enter the permutation as a comma-separated list.

solutions.title: Work down from the largest number
solutions.body:
Note that the condition is symmetric: if $p(k)=j$ then $j+p^{-1}(j)=j+k$, so $p^{-1}$ has the same property.

**Numbers $12$–$20$.** For $16\le k\le20$, $k+p(k)\in[k+1,k+20]\subseteq[17,40]$, which contains only the power $32$. So $p(20)=12$, $p(19)=13$, $p(18)=14$, $p(17)=15$, $p(16)=16$. Applying the same to $p^{-1}$: the value $20$ must come from $12$, $19$ from $13$, $18$ from $14$, $17$ from $15$, i.e. $p(12)=20$, $p(13)=19$, $p(14)=18$, $p(15)=17$. So $p$ maps $\{12,\dots,20\}$ onto itself and therefore maps $\{1,\dots,11\}$ onto itself.

**Numbers $5$–$11$.** Now $p(k)\le11$ for $k\le11$. For $8\le k\le11$, $k+p(k)\in[9,22]$, containing only $16$: $p(11)=5$, $p(10)=6$, $p(9)=7$, $p(8)=8$; and by the symmetry $p(5)=11$, $p(6)=10$, $p(7)=9$. So $p$ maps $\{1,2,3,4\}$ onto itself.

**Numbers $1$–$4$.** $4+p(4)\in[5,8]$ forces $p(4)=4$. Then $3+p(3)\in[4,6]$ forces $p(3)=1$, and by symmetry $p(1)=3$, leaving $p(2)=2$.

Every value was forced, so there is at most one such permutation, and the resulting one works ($1+3=2+2=3+1=4$; $4+4=8$; $5+11=\dots=11+5=16$; $12+20=\dots=20+12=32$):
$$(p(1),\dots,p(20))=(3,2,1,4,11,10,9,8,7,6,5,20,19,18,17,16,15,14,13,12).$$
∎

prompt: We wish to tile a strip of $n$ 1-inch by 1-inch squares. We can use dominos which are made up of two tiles which cover two adjacent squares, or 1-inch square tiles which cover one square. We may cover each square with one or two tiles and a tile can be above or below a domino on a square, but no part of a domino can be placed on any part of a different domino. We do not distinguish whether a domino is above or below a tile on a given square. Let $t(n)$ denote the number of ways the strip can be tiled according to the above rules. Thus for example, $t(1)=2$ and $t(2)=8$. Find a recurrence relation for $t(n)$, and use it to compute $t(6)$.

solutions.title: Look at the last square (official)
solutions.body:
Put $t(0)=1$ (the empty strip). Consider the last square, square $n$.

* **No domino covers square $n$.** Then it carries one or two square tiles ($2$ choices), and squares $1,\dots,n-1$ form an arbitrary tiling: $2t(n-1)$ ways.
* **A domino covers squares $n-1,n$.** No other domino may touch these squares, and each of them may additionally carry one square tile or not ($2\cdot2=4$ choices); squares $1,\dots,n-2$ form an arbitrary tiling: $4t(n-2)$ ways.

Hence
$$t(n)=2t(n-1)+4t(n-2)\qquad(n\ge2).$$
Check: $t(2)=2\cdot2+4\cdot1=8$. Then
$$t(3)=2\cdot8+4\cdot2=24,\quad t(4)=2\cdot24+4\cdot8=80,\quad t(5)=2\cdot80+4\cdot24=256,\quad t(6)=2\cdot256+4\cdot80=832.$$
**Answer:** $t(6)=832$.

solutions.title: Closed form via Fibonacci numbers
solutions.body:
First choose where the dominoes go: a set of pairwise disjoint adjacent pairs, i.e. a tiling of the strip by "monomers and dimers". The number of such choices is the Fibonacci number $F_{n+1}$ ($F_1=F_2=1$), since the last cell is either free ($F_n$ ways for the rest) or the end of a domino ($F_{n-1}$ ways).

Then each square independently has exactly $2$ options: a square not under a domino gets $1$ or $2$ tiles; a square under a domino gets $0$ or $1$ extra tile. So
$$t(n)=2^nF_{n+1},$$
giving $t(1)=2$, $t(2)=4\cdot2=8$ and $t(6)=64\cdot F_7=64\cdot13=832$. (Also $2^nF_{n+1}=2\cdot2^{n-1}F_n+4\cdot2^{n-2}F_{n-1}$, which is the recurrence above.) **Answer: $832$.**

prompt: A cubical box with sides of length $7$ has vertices at $(0,0,0)$, $(7,0,0)$, $(0,7,0)$, $(7,7,0)$, $(0,0,7)$, $(7,0,7)$, $(0,7,7)$, $(7,7,7)$. The inside of the box is lined with mirrors and from the point $(0,1,2)$, a beam of light is directed to the point $(1,3,4)$. The light then reflects repeatedly off the mirrors on the inside of the box. Determine how far the beam of light travels before it first returns to its starting point at $(0,1,2)$.

solutions.title: Unfold the reflections
solutions.body:
A reflection in a face $x=0$ or $x=7$ just reverses the $x$-component of the velocity, and similarly for $y$, $z$. So each coordinate moves independently like a ball bouncing between $0$ and $7$: if the unfolded straight-line motion is $u(s)=(0,1,2)+s(1,2,2)$, the actual position is $(\phi(u_1),\phi(u_2),\phi(u_3))$, where $\phi$ folds $\mathbb R$ onto $[0,7]$: $\phi(u)=u\bmod14$ if that is $\le7$, and $14-(u\bmod14)$ otherwise. The distance travelled is $|s|\cdot|(1,2,2)|=3s$.

The beam is back at $(0,1,2)$ exactly when
$$\phi(s)=0,\qquad \phi(1+2s)=1,\qquad\phi(2+2s)=2.$$
The first condition means $s\equiv0\pmod{14}$. For $s=14$: $1+28=29\equiv1$ and $2+28=30\equiv2\pmod{14}$, so all three hold. Hence the first return is at $s=14$, after a distance $3\cdot14=42$.

(The beam never hits an edge, where the reflection would be ambiguous: that would need two of $s,\ 1+2s,\ 2+2s$ to be multiples of $7$ simultaneously, which never happens for $0<s<14$ — e.g. $s\equiv0$ forces $1+2s\equiv1$, $2+2s\equiv2\pmod7$, and $1+2s$, $2+2s$ differ by $1$.)

**Answer: $42$.**

solutions.title: Track the $x$-coordinate (official)
solutions.body:
The direction is $(1,2,2)$, of length $3$, so the $x$-coordinate changes at $\frac13$ of the speed of the beam, and $y,z$ at $\frac23$ of it. The $x$-coordinate must go from $0$ to $7$ and back to $0$ before the beam can return, i.e. travel $14$ in $x$ (this is the first time $x=0$ again). During that time $y$ and $z$ each travel $28=2\cdot14$, i.e. two full round trips, so they are back at $1$ and $2$ as well. The distance is
$$\sqrt{14^2+28^2+28^2}=14\sqrt{1+4+4}=42.$$
**Answer: $42$.**

prompt: Define $f(x,y)=\dfrac{xy}{x^2+(y\ln(x^2))^2}$ if $x\neq0$, and $f(0,y)=0$ if $y\neq0$. Determine whether $\lim_{(x,y)\to(0,0)}f(x,y)$ exists, and what its value is if the limit does exist.

solutions.title: Bound by AM-GM (official)
solutions.body:
Restrict to $0<|x|<1$, so that $\ln(x^2)\neq0$, and put $z=y\ln(x^2)$. Then $y=\frac{z}{\ln(x^2)}$ and
$$f(x,y)=\frac{xz}{(x^2+z^2)\ln(x^2)}.$$
Since $|xz|\le\frac12(x^2+z^2)$, this gives
$$|f(x,y)|\le\frac1{2|\ln(x^2)|}\qquad(0<|x|<1,\ (x,y)\ne(0,0)).$$
On the line $x=0$ we have $f=0$. As $(x,y)\to(0,0)$, $|\ln(x^2)|\to\infty$ whenever $x\ne0$, so $\frac1{2|\ln x^2|}\to0$. Given $\varepsilon>0$, choose $\delta<e^{-1/(4\varepsilon)}$, $\delta<1$; then for $0<\|(x,y)\|<\delta$ either $x=0$ and $f=0$, or $|\ln x^2|>\frac1{2\varepsilon}$ and $|f|<\varepsilon$.

Hence **the limit exists and equals $0$.**

(The question is tricky because along curves like $y=\frac{x}{\ln(x^2)}$ the denominator is $2x^2$, so $f=\frac{1}{2\ln(x^2)}$, which tends to $0$ only logarithmically slowly.)

solutions.title: Area of a rectangle (official)
solutions.body:
Consider the rectangle $0\le x\le1$, $0\le y\le e$, and the increasing curve $y=e^{x^2}$ from $(0,1)$ to $(1,e)$. It splits the rectangle into the region $B$ below the curve and the region $A$ above it, with $\operatorname{area}(A)+\operatorname{area}(B)=e$.

* $\operatorname{area}(B)=\int_0^1e^{x^2}dx$.
* Describing $A$ by horizontal slices: for $1\le y\le e$ the curve is at $x=\sqrt{\ln y}$, and $A$ consists of the points with $0\le x\le\sqrt{\ln y}$ (for $0\le y<1$ there is nothing above the curve to the left). So $\operatorname{area}(A)=\int_1^e\sqrt{\ln y}\,dy$.

In the last integral substitute $y=1+(e-1)x$, $dy=(e-1)\,dx$, $x\in[0,1]$:
$$\int_1^e\sqrt{\ln y}\,dy=\int_0^1(e-1)\sqrt{\ln(1+ex-x)}\,dx.$$
So the given integral is $\operatorname{area}(A)+\operatorname{area}(B)=e$.

**Answer: $e$.**

solutions.title: Substitution and integration by parts
solutions.body:
Let $I_1=\int_0^1(e-1)\sqrt{\ln(1+(e-1)x)}\,dx$. With $y=1+(e-1)x$, $I_1=\int_1^e\sqrt{\ln y}\,dy$. Now put $y=e^{u^2}$, $u\in[0,1]$, $dy=2ue^{u^2}du$:
$$I_1=\int_0^1u\cdot2ue^{u^2}\,du=\Big[u\,e^{u^2}\Big]_0^1-\int_0^1e^{u^2}\,du=e-\int_0^1e^{u^2}\,du$$
(integration by parts with $U=u$, $dV=2ue^{u^2}du$, $V=e^{u^2}$). Therefore
$$\int_0^1\left((e-1)\sqrt{\ln(1+ex-x)}+e^{x^2}\right)dx=I_1+\int_0^1e^{x^2}dx=e.$$
(Numerically both pieces are $\approx1.2556$ and $\approx1.4627$.) **Answer: $e$.**

prompt: Let $A$ be a $5\times10$ matrix with real entries, and let $A'$ denote its transpose (so $A'$ is a $10\times5$ matrix, and the $ij$th entry of $A'$ is the $ji$th entry of $A$). Suppose every $5\times1$ matrix with real entries (i.e. column vector in $5$ dimensions) can be written in the form $A\mathbf u$ where $\mathbf u$ is a $10\times1$ matrix with real entries. Prove that every $5\times1$ matrix with real entries can be written in the form $AA'\mathbf v$ where $\mathbf v$ is a $5\times1$ matrix with real entries.
answer: $AA'\mathbf x=\mathbf0\Rightarrow\|A'\mathbf x\|^2=\mathbf x'AA'\mathbf x=0\Rightarrow A'\mathbf x=\mathbf0\Rightarrow\mathbf x=\mathbf0$ (as $\operatorname{rank}A'=\operatorname{rank}A=5$), so the $5\times5$ matrix $AA'$ is invertible.

solutions.title: Null spaces (official)
solutions.body:
By hypothesis the column space of $A$ is all of $\mathbb R^5$, so $\operatorname{rank}A=5$, hence $\operatorname{rank}A'=5$ and $A':\mathbb R^5\to\mathbb R^{10}$ is injective (its null space has dimension $5-5=0$).

Suppose $AA'\mathbf x=\mathbf0$ for some $\mathbf x\in\mathbb R^5$. Then
$$0=\mathbf x'AA'\mathbf x=(A'\mathbf x)'(A'\mathbf x)=\|A'\mathbf x\|^2,$$
and since the entries of $A'\mathbf x$ are real, $A'\mathbf x=\mathbf0$, so $\mathbf x=\mathbf0$. Thus the square $5\times5$ matrix $AA'$ has trivial null space, hence is invertible. For any $\mathbf b\in\mathbb R^5$, $\mathbf v=(AA')^{-1}\mathbf b$ gives $AA'\mathbf v=\mathbf b$. ∎

solutions.title: Orthogonal decomposition
solutions.body:
In $\mathbb R^{10}$, the null space of $A$ is the orthogonal complement of the row space of $A$, which is the column space of $A'$: $\mathbf n\perp A'\mathbf v$ for all $\mathbf v$ iff $\mathbf v'A\mathbf n=0$ for all $\mathbf v$ iff $A\mathbf n=\mathbf0$. Hence $\mathbb R^{10}=\operatorname{col}(A')\oplus\operatorname{null}(A)$.

Given $\mathbf b\in\mathbb R^5$, the hypothesis provides $\mathbf u$ with $A\mathbf u=\mathbf b$. Decompose $\mathbf u=A'\mathbf v+\mathbf n$ with $A\mathbf n=\mathbf0$. Then
$$\mathbf b=A\mathbf u=AA'\mathbf v+A\mathbf n=AA'\mathbf v.$$
∎
